parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 2. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a man asking a friend about a scheme that helps people to save energy at home. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5. Ben: Lucy, you had someone round to look at your house last winter, didn't you? About energy, I mean. Our heating bills have gone up so much, and the house still feels cold. Lucy: Oh, yes. That was the Home Energy Scheme. It's run by the council, and it's free. I'd definitely recommend it. Ben: What's the idea behind it? Is it just about cutting bills? Lucy: That's part of it, of course. But the main thing they talk about is making your home more comfortable. Some people think it'll add to the value of the house, but they don't really promise anything like that. Ben: Right. So what happens? Someone comes and does a survey? Lucy: Yes, an adviser comes round for about an hour. The first thing he looked at in our house was the boiler. He wanted to know how old it was, because the older ones waste a lot of energy. He didn't bother with the cooker or anything like that, just the heating system. Ben: Ours is ancient, so that'll be interesting. Lucy: Then you'll definitely want the survey. Before he came, they sent us a short form asking how many people live in the house and how often the heating is on, so have that information ready. Ben: That's easy enough. How long did the whole visit take? Lucy: About an hour, like I said, although he stayed a bit longer because I kept asking questions. He was very patient, and he explained everything in plain English, which I appreciated. Lucy: Then he went up into the loft to see how much insulation there was. We had hardly any, as it turned out. After that, he checked the windows. Our front door is quite new, so he didn't worry about that, but he said the windows at the back were in quite bad condition. Ben: OK. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10. Ben: Did he look at anything else? Lucy: Yes, he checked for damp. We had a patch in the bathroom, and he said that can make a house much harder to heat. And the clever part was that he used a special camera. It shows exactly where the heat is escaping. I'd assumed he'd bring some kind of meter, but the camera was much better. You could see the gaps round the windows glowing on the screen. Ben: Amazing. And after the survey, do they actually help you pay for anything? Lucy: They do. There's a grant for a new heating system. It used to cover up to fifty per cent of the cost, but they've just raised it to sixty per cent. Ben: So sixty per cent now. That's really generous. Lucy: It is. They also give you a free smart thermostat, so you can control the heating from your phone. They used to hand out free light bulbs as well, but they've stopped doing that. Ben: I'd like the thermostat, anyway. Lucy: And the adviser also gave us a lot of tips on saving water, which surprised me, because I thought it would all be about gas and electricity. But heating water uses a lot of energy. Ben: That makes sense. Is there a deadline for applying? Lucy: Yes. The leaflet says the end of October, but I saw on the website that they've extended it until the end of November. Ben: The end of November. Great, I'll apply this week. Thanks, Lucy. Oh, and one more thing. Do you have to be a homeowner, or can people who rent apply as well? Lucy: Tenants can apply too, but they need the landlord's permission for any building work. The advice and the thermostat are available to everyone. Ben: Good to know. My brother rents a flat, so I'll tell him about it. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a summer sports camp talking to a group of new staff. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Rachel: Good morning, everyone. I'm Rachel Moore, and I manage the Riverside Summer Sports Camp. Thank you all for joining us this year. Most of the children who come to us are between seven and twelve, and our aim is simply for them to be active, make friends and enjoy themselves. Many of them come back year after year, and some of our staff were campers here themselves when they were younger, which I think says a lot about the place. Rachel: I'd like to start by explaining what you'll be doing during a typical day. The children arrive between half past eight and nine. Parents drop them at the main gate, and your job there is to check each child's name against the list, so that we know exactly who's on site. Please don't get involved in collecting payments. That's all handled by the office. Rachel: Our tennis sessions are run by qualified coaches, so you won't be teaching. What we need you to do is hand out the rackets and balls at the start, and make sure they all come back at the end. Rachel: In the team games, like football and rounders, your main job is to organise the teams so that they're fair. Children can get very upset if one side has all the best players, so mix them up carefully. Rachel: Swimming is also taught by specialist coaches. But we need staff to supervise the children in the changing rooms, before and after each session. That's where things can easily go wrong if nobody's watching. Rachel: After lunch, when the afternoon sessions begin, you'll be responsible for leading the warm-up exercises. We'll show you a routine during training, and it's the same every day, so it's easy to learn. You don't need to serve lunch, by the way. The kitchen staff do that. Lunch itself is at half past twelve in the main hall, and you'll eat with the children, which is a good chance to get to know them. Rachel: And at the end of each week, you'll fill in a short progress chart for each child in your group, which we then send home to parents. Please don't phone parents yourselves. If there's a problem, tell me or one of the team leaders. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Rachel: Now, some practical matters. Football is by far our most popular activity, and more children sign up for it than for anything else. But it actually needs fewer staff than swimming, because in the pool we have to keep to a strict ratio of one adult to every six children. Tennis sessions are the longest, but they're in small groups, so they don't need many of you. So swimming is actually where we need the most people. We usually have around a hundred and twenty children each week, although numbers are always highest in August. Rachel: People often ask me what we're looking for in our staff. Being good at sport is useful, of course, and we expect you to be on time every day. But the most important thing by far is patience. Children don't always listen, and some of them will be nervous or homesick, especially in the first week. Rachel: You'll also find that no two days are the same. The weather here can change quickly, and if it rains, we move as many activities as possible into the sports hall, so be ready to adapt. Rachel: As for dates, your training takes place on Monday the fourteenth of July, here in the sports hall. The children arrive for the first time a week later, on Monday the twenty-first, so that's when you'll start working with them. Then, in the week beginning the twenty-eighth, I'll meet each of you individually to see how things are going. Rachel: Finally, at the end of the summer, we always do something to thank our staff. For several years we held a sports tournament, staff against coaches, and last year we had a trip to the coast. This year, we've booked a meal at a restaurant in town, on the last Friday in August. I hope you'll all be able to come. Rachel: Right, let's go and have a look at the sports hall. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two media studies students called Priya and Jake discussing possible topics for their project. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25. Priya: Jake, we really need to decide on a topic for our media project. The proposal's due next week. Jake: I know. Let's go through the areas we've covered this term and see which ones might work. Priya: Good idea. And we should pick something we'll both enjoy, because we'll be working on it for the whole term. Jake: Absolutely. Last term I chose a topic just because it seemed easy, and I was bored with it after two weeks. Priya: OK. What about advertising? There'd be a lot of statistics about spending and audiences. Jake: True, and at least there's loads of material out there. We'd have no trouble finding examples online. Priya: That's a point in its favour. What about video games? I'd never really thought of them as media until that seminar with Dr Okoro. Jake: The one about how games tell stories? That was brilliant. I came out with so many ideas. Priya: Me too. Then there's film censorship. I thought it would be interesting to look at how rules on what films can show have changed. Jake: Hmm, isn't that one of the topics they've dropped from the course this year? Someone in my tutorial said it had been moved to the second-year syllabus. Priya: Really? I'm not sure, but we probably shouldn't risk it. Jake: I'll check with the course office anyway. It would be a shame if it's still allowed. Jake: What about radio? We had that lecture on it last week. Priya: I didn't get much from that, to be honest. It was so general. The lecturer never really looked at any particular stations or programmes. Jake: No, I hardly wrote anything down either. Priya: And celebrity news? That's everywhere at the moment. Jake: It is, but a lot of the stories come from anonymous sources, and some of them are just made up. We'd have to be really careful about what we could trust. Priya: That's true. Jake: So none of those seems perfect, does it? Priya: Not really. Let's think about it from a different angle. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30. Priya: Actually, there's something we haven't considered: podcasts. They've grown so fast in the last few years, and nearly everyone I know listens to them. Jake: Good idea. Let's do that. In my family, it's actually my grandfather who listens to them most. My parents hardly ever do, and my brother only watches videos. Priya: Your grandfather? That's unexpected. Jake: He says it's like the radio used to be, but he can choose what he wants. Priya: That's lovely. My mum listens to them while she's cooking, but I mostly listen when I'm at the gym. Jake: Anyway, what about recent changes? A lot of podcasts are now filmed as well, so you can watch them as videos. Priya: I really like that. You can see the people talking, and you can still just listen if you're busy. Jake: Same here. It's much better than the longer episodes they seem to be making now. Some of them go on for three hours. Priya: I know, and there are far more adverts than there used to be. What about amateur podcasts? Anyone can make one now. Jake: That's the good thing about them, but it also means nobody checks what's said. People can repeat things that simply aren't true. Priya: Yes, I think that's a real danger. We should include something about that. Jake: We should also mention Serial, the crime podcast from 2014. It looked again at a murder case, and it's often given as an example of a podcast that had an influence on a real legal case. Priya: Definitely. It was also one of the first podcasts to attract a really huge audience, but let's focus on the legal side. Jake: OK. And we could look at listening figures. There's plenty of data on how many people download each episode. Priya: But what I'm not sure about is how many people actually listen to the end. A download doesn't mean someone's heard the whole thing. I'll try to find out. Jake: Good. So I think we've got a plan. Priya: Yes. Shall we meet again on Thursday to start writing the proposal? Jake: Thursday's fine. I'll book a room in the library. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about how travel destinations become fashionable. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I want to look at trends in tourism. Just like clothes or food, holiday destinations go in and out of fashion, and in recent years, the speed at which this happens has increased enormously. Tourism is now one of the largest industries in the world, and before the pandemic, international tourist arrivals had passed one billion a year. So these changes in fashion have real economic consequences. Lecturer: A generation ago, most people chose where to go on holiday by looking through brochures or asking friends. Today, research shows that many travellers make their decision after seeing images of a place online, often on social media. A single striking photograph of a mountain lake or a colourful street can bring thousands of visitors to a place that was almost unknown the year before. Lecturer: The travel industry responds to this very quickly. When a destination starts to become popular, budget airlines are often the first to react, adding new routes within a few months. Tour operators, meanwhile, pay social media influencers to visit and post about their holidays. Many hotels and resorts now employ staff whose only job is to follow what's trending online. Lecturer: Let's look at some examples of places whose popularity has been shaped by the media. New Zealand is a well-known case. After a series of fantasy films was shot there, the number of visitors rose sharply, and the country's tourism organisation made the most of it. Many fans travelled specifically to see the filming locations, and some of these have become major attractions in their own right. Lecturer: Iceland provides a rather different example. In 2010, ash from a volcano disrupted flights across Europe for several days, and the country was worried that tourists would be put off. So it launched a campaign that asked Icelanders themselves to share stories about their country online, and to invite visitors to experience it. The campaign was remarkably successful, and tourist numbers grew rapidly over the following decade. Some visitors now come in winter to see the northern lights, which has helped to spread tourism across the year. Lecturer: Television can have a similar effect. In Scotland, a popular historical drama series led to a big increase in visits to the castles where it was filmed, and some sites that had previously attracted only a few visitors suddenly found themselves overwhelmed. Lecturer: This brings me to the downside of these trends. Popularity can bring enormous benefits to local economies, but it can also cause serious damage. One famous example is Maya Bay in Thailand, which became extremely popular after it appeared in a Hollywood film. So many boats and visitors arrived every day that the authorities closed the bay completely in 2018, to allow the coral to recover. It reopened a few years later, but with strict limits on visitor numbers. Lecturer: Venice is another city that has struggled with its own popularity. For years, huge cruise ships sailed close to the historic centre, and in 2021 large cruise ships were banned from entering the city's main canal. But the problem isn't only the number of visitors. Many apartments in the city are now rented to tourists on a short-term basis, and as a result, rents have risen so much that many local people can no longer afford to live there. Lecturer: In response, some destinations are now trying to manage their popularity. Venice, for instance, has started charging day visitors an entry fee at busy times of the year, and other cities are encouraging tourists to explore less well-known neighbourhoods, so that the benefits, and the pressures, are shared more evenly. Whether these measures will be enough is a question we'll return to next week. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

We'll show you a routine during training, and it's the same every day, so it's easy to learn. You don't need to serve lunch, by the way. The kitchen staff do that. Lunch itself is at half past twelve in the main hall, and you'll eat with the children, which is a good chance to get to know them. Rachel: And at the end of each week, you'll fill in a short progress chart for each child in your group, which we then send home to parents. Please don't phone parents yourselves. If there's a problem, tell me or one of the team leaders. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Rachel: Now, some practical matters. Football is by far our most popular activity, and more children sign up for it than for anything else. But it actually needs fewer staff than swimming, because in the pool we have to keep to a strict ratio of one adult to every six children. Tennis sessions are the longest, but they're in small groups, so they don't need many of you. So swimming is actually where we need the most people. We usually have around a hundred and twenty children each week, although numbers are always highest in August. Rachel: People often ask me what we're looking for in our staff. Being good at sport is useful, of course, and we expect you to be on time every day. But the most important thing by far is patience. Children don't always listen, and some of them will be nervous or homesick, especially in the first week. Rachel: You'll also find that no two days are the same. The weather here can change quickly, and if it rains, we move as many activities as possible into the sports hall, so be ready to adapt. Rachel: As for dates, your training takes place on Monday the fourteenth of July, here in the sports hall. The children arrive for the first time a week later, on Monday the twenty-first, so that's when you'll start working with them. Then, in the week beginning the twenty-eighth, I'll meet each of you individually to see how things are going. Rachel: Finally, at the end of the summer, we always do something to thank our staff. For several years we held a sports tournament, staff against coaches, and last year we had a trip to the coast. This year, we've booked a meal at a restaurant in town, on the last Friday in August. I hope you'll all be able to come. Rachel: Right, let's go and have a look at the sports hall. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two media studies students called Priya and Jake discussing possible topics for their project. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25. Priya: Jake, we really need to decide on a topic for our media project. The proposal's due next week. Jake: I know. Let's go through the areas we've covered this term and see which ones might work. Priya: Good idea. And we should pick something we'll both enjoy, because we'll be working on it for the whole term. Jake: Absolutely. Last term I chose a topic just because it seemed easy, and I was bored with it after two weeks. Priya: OK. What about advertising? There'd be a lot of statistics about spending and audiences. Jake: True, and at least there's loads of material out there. We'd have no trouble finding examples online. Priya: That's a point in its favour. What about video games? I'd never really thought of them as media until that seminar with Dr Okoro. Jake: The one about how games tell stories? That was brilliant. I came out with so many ideas. Priya: Me too. Then there's film censorship. I thought it would be interesting to look at how rules on what films can show have changed. Jake: Hmm, isn't that one of the topics they've dropped from the course this year? Someone in my tutorial said it had been moved to the second-year syllabus. Priya: Really? I'm not sure, but we probably shouldn't risk it. Jake: I'll check with the course office anyway. It would be a shame if it's still allowed. Jake: What about radio? We had that lecture on it last week. Priya: I didn't get much from that, to be honest. It was so general. The lecturer never really looked at any particular stations or programmes. Jake: No, I hardly wrote anything down either. Priya: And celebrity news? That's everywhere at the moment. Jake: It is, but a lot of the stories come from anonymous sources, and some of them are just made up. We'd have to be really careful about what we could trust. Priya: That's true. Jake: So none of those seems perfect, does it? Priya: Not really. Let's think about it from a different angle. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30. Priya: Actually, there's something we haven't considered: podcasts. They've grown so fast in the last few years, and nearly everyone I know listens to them. Jake: Good idea. Let's do that. In my family, it's actually my grandfather who listens to them most. My parents hardly ever do, and my brother only watches videos. Priya: Your grandfather? That's unexpected. Jake: He says it's like the radio used to be, but he can choose what he wants. Priya: That's lovely. My mum listens to them while she's cooking, but I mostly listen when I'm at the gym. Jake: Anyway, what about recent changes? A lot of podcasts are now filmed as well, so you can watch them as videos. Priya: I really like that. You can see the people talking, and you can still just listen if you're busy. Jake: Same here. It's much better than the longer episodes they seem to be making now. Some of them go on for three hours. Priya: I know, and there are far more adverts than there used to be. What about amateur podcasts? Anyone can make one now. Jake: That's the good thing about them, but it also means nobody checks what's said. People can repeat things that simply aren't true. Priya: Yes, I think that's a real danger. We should include something about that. Jake: We should also mention Serial, the crime podcast from 2014. It looked again at a murder case, and it's often given as an example of a podcast that had an influence on a real legal case. Priya: Definitely. It was also one of the first podcasts to attract a really huge audience, but let's focus on the legal side. Jake: OK. And we could look at listening figures. There's plenty of data on how many people download each episode. Priya: But what I'm not sure about is how many people actually listen to the end. A download doesn't mean someone's heard the whole thing. I'll try to find out. Jake: Good. So I think we've got a plan. Priya: Yes. Shall we meet again on Thursday to start writing the proposal? Jake: Thursday's fine. I'll book a room in the library. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of a lecture about how travel destinations become fashionable. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I want to look at trends in tourism. Just like clothes or food, holiday destinations go in and out of fashion, and in recent years, the speed at which this happens has increased enormously. Tourism is now one of the largest industries in the world, and before the pandemic, international tourist arrivals had passed one billion a year. So these changes in fashion have real economic consequences. Lecturer: A generation ago, most people chose where to go on holiday by looking through brochures or asking friends. Today, research shows that many travellers make their decision after seeing images of a place online, often on social media. A single striking photograph of a mountain lake or a colourful street can bring thousands of visitors to a place that was almost unknown the year before. Lecturer: The travel industry responds to this very quickly. When a destination starts to become popular, budget airlines are often the first to react, adding new routes within a few months. Tour operators, meanwhile, pay social media influencers to visit and post about their holidays. Many hotels and resorts now employ staff whose only job is to follow what's trending online. Lecturer: Let's look at some examples of places whose popularity has been shaped by the media. New Zealand is a well-known case. After a series of fantasy films was shot there, the number of visitors rose sharply, and the country's tourism organisation made the most of it. Many fans travelled specifically to see the filming locations, and some of these have become major attractions in their own right. Lecturer: Iceland provides a rather different example. In 2010, ash from a volcano disrupted flights across Europe for several days, and the country was worried that tourists would be put off. So it launched a campaign that asked Icelanders themselves to share stories about their country online, and to invite visitors to experience it. The campaign was remarkably successful, and tourist numbers grew rapidly over the following decade. Some visitors now come in winter to see the northern lights, which has helped to spread tourism across the year. Lecturer: Television can have a similar effect. In Scotland, a popular historical drama series led to a big increase in visits to the castles where it was filmed, and some sites that had previously attracted only a few visitors suddenly found themselves overwhelmed. Lecturer: This brings me to the downside of these trends. Popularity can bring enormous benefits to local economies, but it can also cause serious damage. One famous example is Maya Bay in Thailand, which became extremely popular after it appeared in a Hollywood film. So many boats and visitors arrived every day that the authorities closed the bay completely in 2018, to allow the coral to recover. It reopened a few years later, but with strict limits on visitor numbers. Lecturer: Venice is another city that has struggled with its own popularity. For years, huge cruise ships sailed close to the historic centre, and in 2021 large cruise ships were banned from entering the city's main canal. But the problem isn't only the number of visitors. Many apartments in the city are now rented to tourists on a short-term basis, and as a result, rents have risen so much that many local people can no longer afford to live there. Lecturer: In response, some destinations are now trying to manage their popularity. Venice, for instance, has started charging day visitors an entry fee at busy times of the year, and other cities are encouraging tourists to explore less well-known neighbourhoods, so that the benefits, and the pressures, are shared more evenly. Whether these measures will be enough is a question we'll return to next week. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
